pdf_context: Overall assessment My overall conclusion is positive: the study has a strong core idea and a meaningful contribution. In particular, the central framing that thermal physiology in dynamic environments may be better understood as a latent dynamical process rather than a static stimulus-response mapping is both interesting and scientifically worthwhile. The combination of a discrete model (IO- HMM) and a continuous model (LDS) is a good conceptual choice, and the COC dataset is well suited to studying physiological dynamics in ecologically realistic hot commuting conditions. At the same time, I think the paper is currently strongest as: an exploratory latent-state analysis of thermophysiological dynamics under naturalistic thermal exposure, interpreted using external comfort proxies and weaker as: a fully validated thermal sensation inference framework The main reason is simple: COC does not contain direct TSV labels. Main scientific conclusion Does the COC dataset validate the whole pipeline? My answer is: not fully. What COC does support well The COC dataset does support: latent-state discovery from multimodal physiology analysis of dynamic physiological transitions examination of transient volatility around state changes interpretation of latent states using external reference quantities such as ACD and transferred pseudo-TSV This is consistent with the manuscript’s broader motivation that dynamic thermal perception should be studied as a time-evolving physiological process rather than as a static instantaneous mapping. What COC does not validate directly The COC dataset does not directly validate: subjective thermal sensation prediction in the target domain the accuracy of pseudo-TSV transfer in COC the full end-to-end perceptual interpretation of the latent states The reason is that the manuscript itself states that no TSV were collected in COC. This is described in the dataset section of manuscript/COC_manu.pdf , and the repository also reflects this by relying on transferred pseudo-TSV from TSD/CQU rather than target-domain labels. So I think the paper should avoid language that reads as if COC provides direct validation of sensation inference. It provides strong support for exploratory physiological state analysis, but only indirect support for sensation interpretation. What I think is already strong 1. The conceptual framing The manuscript’s core idea is compelling: thermal experience in dynamic settings is state-dependent physiology is not just a predictor, but a mediator latent-state modeling is a reasonable framework for this problem This framing is consistent across the Introduction, Methods, and the overall repository structure. 2. The use of two complementary proxies I think the use of both: transferred pseudo-TSV Adaptive Comfort Deviation (ACD) is a sensible strategy given the absence of target-domain TSV. In particular, the adaptive comfort route gives the paper a theory-based benchmark independent of the transfer-learning model. The TSD/CQU validation in utils/adaptive_comfort_analysis.py and the manuscript discussion around ACD-TSV monotonicity are useful and strengthen the proxy argument. 3. The latent-state analysis itself The repository clearly implements a substantial latent-state analysis stack: preprocessing and feature construction in thermal_state_pipeline.py IO-HMM in utils/ssm_io_hmm.py LDS machinery via utils/thermal_state_model.py post hoc interpretation through utils/plot_hmm_state_semantics.py , utils/analyze_hmm_deep.py , utils/transient_index_analysis.py , utils/plot_ti_with_settling.py , and utils/plot_lds_dim_velocity.py This is not a superficial analysis. The codebase does support a serious attempt to characterize physiological state structure and transitions. Main issues that I think should be clarified before submission 1. The manuscript describes a pooled IO-HMM, but the default pipeline runs per-subject HMMs This is the largest methods-implementation issue I found. The manuscript states that the IO-HMM was trained on the full consolidated in-car dataset with one shared model. This is stated explicitly in the methods section of manuscript/COC_manu.pdf , where the text says the observations are “z-scored by a global pooled scaler before fitting a single shared model.” That pooled behavior does exist in the codebase: utils/ssm_io_hmm.py contains a dedicated run_pooled() function However, the main pipeline currently calls: run_subjects() from thermal_state_pipeline.py Specifically: thermal_state_pipeline.py -> run_hmm_all_subjects() calls utils.ssm_io_hmm.run_subjects() this routine fits a separate HMM per subject Why this matters: if the manuscript figures and tables come from a pooled model, that needs to be the documented and reproducible path if the current default pipeline is the intended path, then the manuscript description of a pooled model is inaccurate I think this is a fixable issue, but it should be resolved clearly because it affects the meaning of the latent states. 2. The saved viterbi_state is not actually a Viterbi path The manuscript repeatedly refers to “Viterbi-decoded” state transitions. In the code, however, the state sequence saved to posteriors.csv is generated by: computing posterior probabilities gamma taking argmax at each time point In utils/ssm_io_hmm.py , the relevant line is effectively: states = gamma.argmax(axis=1) This is not the same as a full Viterbi path. Why I think this matters: pointwise posterior argmax can generate more jittery transitions transition timing can shift transition counts can inflate downstream transient analyses depend directly on these transitions This does not invalidate the entire paper, but I do think the manuscript should either: use true Viterbi decoding, or relabel the method accurately and revisit any claims tied to transition structure 3. State ordering is not fully stable across the analysis stack One thing I found important is that different scripts infer state order in different ways. Examples: utils/plot_hmm_state_semantics.py orders states using tsv_e utils/transient_index_analysis.py searches for tsv / TSV and then falls back to PMV utils/analyze_hmm_deep.py also falls back to PMV if no TSV-like column exists some manuscript-facing summaries use ACD ordering Why this matters: labels such as S0-S5 may not refer to exactly the same ordering in every figure “warming” and “cooling” transitions can depend on the ranking rule cross-figure interpretation becomes harder to defend I think the paper would benefit from defining one canonical state-ordering rule, ideally one explicitly stated in the manuscript and applied across all downstream scripts. 4. The PMV methods description appears stronger than the preprocessing path actually used The manuscript describes PMV as using: 0.5 clo 1.2 met subject-specific BSA-based metabolic scaling The repository does contain BSA/met-scaling logic in: utils/calc_thermal_index.py However, the main pipeline path for thermal indices goes through: detect_transient_incident.add_thermal_index_timestamp() That path appears to use fixed values rather than individualized BSA scaling. I think this is important because the manuscript currently gives the impression of a more individualized physical model than the main analysis path seems to implement. Again, this is fixable in either direction: revise the code to match the manuscript, or revise the manuscript to match the code 5. The statistical tone should probably be more cautious Several analyses are informative and interesting, but I think they should be described more clearly as exploratory or descriptive unless subject-aware statistical modeling is added. For example: within-state regressions in utils/analyze_hmm_deep.py pool repeated observations across subjects transition statistics in utils/plot_ti_with_settling.py pool per-event distributions across subjects and pairs The patterns may still be real and scientifically useful, but I would hesitate to treat the resulting p-values as strong evidence of general mechanisms without accounting for subject-level dependence. My suggestion is not necessarily to remove these analyses, but to moderate the wording around them. 6. The transition-settling result is interesting, but likely more heuristic than universal The reported settling / departure-time result around roughly 1.2-1.7 minutes is one of the most interesting findings in the draft. However, in the code this quantity is derived from a custom departure detector in: utils/plot_ti_with_settling.py It depends on chosen values for: smoothing width slope reference window threshold fraction sustain length That does not make the result wrong. But I do think the paper should be careful not to present it as a fixed physiological constant unless a sensitivity analysis shows the estimate is robust. 7. A few discussion claims appear stronger than the direct evidence available One example that stood out to me is the discussion statement that the asymmetry between warming and cooling cannot be explained by environmental forcing because ambient temperature-change rates were comparable across directions. I did not find an explicit supporting analysis for that claim in the codebase. So I would suggest either: adding that analysis directly, or softening the statement I also noticed that Figure A.10 in the manuscript appears conceptually inconsistent with the statement that COC has no TSV. That figure and its caption likely need a careful check. How I would frame the paper If I were trying to position the paper as strongly and fairly as possible, I would frame it approximately like this: We introduce a latent-state framework for analyzing thermophysiological dynamics in naturalistic thermal environments. Using physiology from the COC dataset, we identify structured latent regimes and transition patterns, and interpret them using adaptive comfort and transferred pseudo-TSV proxies. Because COC lacks direct TSV labels, the results should be understood as exploratory and proxy-supported rather than as fully validated target-domain sensation inference. I think that framing preserves the novelty of the work while making the evidence harder to challenge. What I would prioritize before submission My suggested order of revision would be: 1. Resolve pooled vs per-subject HMM description and reproducibility. 2. Fix or relabel the viterbi_state issue. 3. Standardize the state ranking rule across all analyses. 4. Align PMV methods with actual implementation. 5. Reframe the validation language around the absence of target-domain TSV. 6. Moderate statistical and mechanistic claims where needed. 7. Check unsupported discussion statements and Appendix figure wording. Final view I want to emphasize that my reading is not that the study is weak. On the contrary, I think the study is promising and the core idea is good. My main concern is that a few of the current claims run slightly ahead of the evidence and the implemented default workflow. If those points are cleaned up, I think the manuscript will become: more reproducible more credible easier to defend in review and, importantly, it will still retain the novelty and value of the latent-state contribution.
